To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the bacterium Shewanella putrfaciens can reduce iron oxides to soluble iron ions, and this reduction can lead to corrosion of carbon steel.
the bacterium Shewanella putrifaciens reduces ferric iron oxides, and the reduction is accompanied by dissolution and mineral replacement.

(1) S. putrefacens can use iron oxides as an electron acceptor; (2) iron oxide bioreduction is a viable process for the treatment of metal-contaminated water and waste; and (3) iron oxide biomineralization can be used to control the corrosion of carbon steel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biogeochemical processes that occur at the interface of a metal and a microbe.
understanding the mechanism(s) of microbial iron reduction and the role of iron oxide biomineralization on corrosion of carbon steel.
the role of biominerals in microbial metal corrosion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

biomineralization can be a factor in microbiologically influenced corrosive processes, and that the mechanism of this effect is through the replacement of the mineral phase by bacterial iron reduction.
the role of iron-reducing bacteria in corrosion of carbon steel is to reduce ferric oxides on the steel surface.
the biomineralization of iron oxides is a critical factor in the process of MIC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of a mineral phase on the steel surface can be beneficial to the corrosion process by acting as a reservoir for ferrous iron and by facilitating the transport of ferrous ions away from the steel surface.
iron oxides are reduced by the metal-reduking bacteria, Shewanella, and the reduction of the oxides leads to corrosion of the underlying steel.
iron reduction by the bacterium was accompanied by mineral dissolution and replacement, resulting in the formation of iron sulfide and iron hydroxides, and ultimately, the corrosion of carbon steel.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of biogenic iron oxides on the surface of steel can be an important factor in MIC.
biomineralization can occur in the absence of organic matter and that this can be used as a tool to study the biogeochemistry of metal oxides.
the mineralogy of the surface films on carbon steels is a key factor in microbiologically influenced carbon steel corrosion.
